title: How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)
text:
In this post I use R to compare average GDP per capita across continents in 1952 and 2007, and to see which continents grew the fastest.
Data: gapminder R package by Jennifer Bryan, an excerpt of data from the Gapminder Foundation (CC BY 4.0). GDP per capita is measured in inflation-adjusted US dollars.

title: How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)
text:
Setup

library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)

section: Average GDP per capita by continent

title: How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)
How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)
text:
Visualise

ggplot(gdp_by_year, aes(x = continent, y = mean_gdp, fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::dollar(mean_gdp)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#F7A6AC", "#EEC78A", "#CBE4B1", "#B8E5FA", "#EEE9A2")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average GDP per capita (US$)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))







Figure 1: Average GDP per capita by continent in 1952 and 2007.

title: How Rich Are the Continents? GDP per Capita, 1952 vs 2007 (R)
text:
What I found
Average GDP per capita grew on every continent between 1952 and 2007, but the gaps between continents became much larger. Oceania was the richest continent in both years, rising from US$10,298 to US$29,810. Europe came second, reaching US$25,054 in 2007. Africa remained by far the poorest: its average rose from US$1,253 to only US$3,089, about a tenth of Oceania’s in 2007.
Europe grew the fastest, with average GDP per capita rising 4.4 times. The other continents grew between 2.4 and 2.9 times. Because Africa started from the lowest level and grew relatively slowly, the absolute gap between Africa and Oceania widened from about US$9,000 in 1952 to almost US$27,000 in 2007.
Averages can be misleading. In 1952, Kuwait had a GDP per capita of about US$108,000 thanks to its oil wealth, more than seven times that of the next richest country, Switzerland (about US$14,700). This single country pulls up Asia’s 1952 average and makes Asia look richer than the Americas, even though most Asian countries were poor at the time. It also helps explain why Asia shows the smallest growth ratio (2.4 times), despite the rapid economic growth of many Asian countries. A median, or looking at individual countries, would give a fuller picture. The data also stop in 2007.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.


My first few weeks in the Master of Data Science program at UBC have been both exhilarating and deeply rewarding. From the engaging orientation events to diving straight into our first week of classes, the transition back to intense academic life was fast-paced, surrounded by a cohort of incredibly talented and supportive peers.
One thing that genuinely surprised me was how quickly we transitioned from high-level concepts to hands-on, practical coding workflows. While the workload is definitely challenging, the collaborative atmosphere and the helpful guidance from instructors make every late-night debugging session feel like a shared victory rather than a lonely struggle.
Overall, I am feeling optimistic and energized about the journey ahead. Although there is still so much more to learn and explore, I am already looking forward to seeing how much my skills will grow by the end of this program.

title: How Big Are Antarctic Penguins? (Python)
text:
In this post I use Python to explore how body size differs across three species of penguins living near Palmer Station, Antarctica.
Data: Palmer Penguins, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. Released under the CC0 licence.

title: How Big Are Antarctic Penguins? (Python)
text:
What I found
After removing penguins with missing values, the data contain 333 penguins: 146 Adelie, 68 Chinstrap, and 119 Gentoo. Gentoo penguins are clearly the largest species, with an average body mass of about 5,092 g. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins are much lighter and almost identical in size, averaging about 3,706 g and 3,733 g respectively. Within every species, males are heavier than females. The gap is largest for Gentoo penguins (about 805 g), followed by Adelie (about 675 g) and Chinstrap penguins (about 412 g).
Flipper length and body mass are strongly and positively correlated, with a correlation of 0.87: penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier. In the scatter plot, Gentoo penguins form their own group in the upper right, with flipper lengths of roughly 205 to 230 mm. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap heavily in the lower left, with most flippers between about 180 and 205 mm. The same upward trend also appears within each species, not only between them.
This means body size alone is enough to pick out a Gentoo penguin, but not to tell an Adelie from a Chinstrap. The data come from three islands over three years, so they may not represent all penguins of these species. A natural next step would be to look at bill length and bill depth, which might help separate Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

When I am not deep into coding or coursework, you can usually find me exploring new hobbies and unwinding. I enjoy creating pixel art with perler beads, traveling to discover new places, and watching films. I am also a big fan of Asian cuisine, especially Japanese and Korean food, and I love trying out different local eateries on the weekends.
